name: Apollo 15 laser mirror
intro: This is the biggest Apollo laser mirror, with 300 glass prisms, three times as many as Apollo 11’s. Dave Scott and Jim Irwin set it up near Hadley Rille in 1971. It needs no power, and laser stations on Earth still aim at it more than at any other Apollo mirror.

hotspots.title: 300 prisms
hotspots.text: Each of these 300 glass prisms bounces laser light straight back toward Earth. More prisms means a brighter echo, which is why observatories love this mirror.

source.label: NASA JPL: Apollo 11 experiment still returns valuable data

photo.alt: Close-up of a large panel of round mirror cells set in a grid, on the grey lunar ground.
photo.caption: Dave Scott’s close-up of the mirror panel after setup.
photo.licenseEvidence: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal image library: NASA Hasselblad frame AS15-85-11468, NASA film scan (not a third-party restoration). NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: Two panels
hotspots.text: The mirror is made of a big panel and a smaller one hinged together, so it could fold up for the trip.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 image library

hotspots.title: Aiming at Earth
hotspots.text: A sun compass and bubble level on the end helped Scott point the mirror at Earth. Scout’s check: nothing here needs power or repairs.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 image library

hotspots.title: Seen from orbit
hotspots.text: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed this landing site from above. The mirror is too small to see, but its spot is marked among the tracks.

source.label: NASA JPL: Apollo 11 experiment still returns valuable data

photo.alt: A grey, cratered surface seen from above with labels for the laser mirror, the science station and the lander.
photo.caption: The Apollo 15 site from orbit, with the laser mirror’s spot labeled.
photo.licenseEvidence: LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are free for educational use with credit; this site is an educational NASA Space Apps project.

funFact: Laser ranging showed that the Moon drifts away from Earth by about 3.8 cm every year.
whyLeft: It was meant to stay forever as a target for lasers fired from Earth.
repurpose: It is still in use. Future Moon bases could check their own positions against it, since its location is known to within centimeters.
